questions.stem: The ruins of Nineveh lie in modern Iraq on the east bank of the Tigris, opposite the city of:
options: Baghdad
Basra
Erbil
Mosul
questions.explanation: Nineveh faces Mosul across the Tigris in northern Iraq, where the Khosr River joins it. Baghdad lies far to the south, near ancient Babylonian territory.

questions.stem: The site of Nineveh is dominated by two large mounds. They are:
options: Khorsabad and Nimrud
Tell Brak and Tell Hamoukar
Babylon and Borsippa
Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus
questions.explanation: Kuyunjik holds the palaces of Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal, and Nebi Yunus held a later arsenal palace beneath a shrine to the prophet Jonah. Khorsabad and Nimrud are separate Assyrian capitals.

questions.stem: Tiglath-Pileser I, a Middle Assyrian king of the late second millennium BCE, is significant in the growth of Assyria because he:
options: campaigned west against the Arameans and reached the Mediterranean
built the first palace on the mound of Nebi Yunus for his army
conquered Egypt and placed Assyrian governors in Memphis and Thebes
made Nineveh the sole capital, ending the role of Ashur for good
questions.explanation: His annals record campaigns across the Euphrates against the Arameans and a march to the Mediterranean coast, setting a pattern later Neo-Assyrian kings followed. Egypt was conquered only in the seventh century BCE.

questions.stem: Sargon II built a new capital, Dur-Sharrukin, at the site now called Khorsabad. What happened to it after his death?
options: It was flooded by the Tigris and rebuilt as a temple city
It was abandoned when Sennacherib moved the capital to Nineveh
It became the main capital of Assyria for the next two hundred years
It was handed to the Babylonians as part of a peace treaty
questions.explanation: Sargon died in battle in 705 BCE and his body was not recovered, and his son Sennacherib chose Nineveh as his capital, leaving Dur-Sharrukin largely unused. Assyria fell less than a century later.

questions.stem: Assyrian kings moved the capital from Ashur to Kalhu (Nimrud), then to Dur-Sharrukin, then to Nineveh. What does this pattern best suggest?
options: The gods of Ashur forbade any king from living there for long
Building a new capital was a way for a king to display his power
Each old capital had been destroyed by enemies before the king moved
Assyrian kings were nomads who never lived in any one city
questions.explanation: New capitals with great palaces and gardens advertised a king's wealth, piety and command of labour and captives. Ashur remained the religious heart of Assyria even after the court moved.

questions.stem: In 1842 Paul-Emile Botta, the French consul at Mosul, dug at Kuyunjik with little success and moved to Khorsabad. What mistake did he make there?
options: He believed the reliefs he found were Egyptian rather than Assyrian
He believed Khorsabad was a Roman fort built on top of a Greek city
He believed the cuneiform tablets were decorative patterns, not writing
He believed the palace he found at Khorsabad was Nineveh
questions.explanation: Botta uncovered Sargon II's palace at Khorsabad and announced it as Nineveh, before cuneiform could be read well enough to identify the site. It was in fact Dur-Sharrukin.

questions.stem: Austen Henry Layard excavated Kuyunjik from the late 1840s. His main discovery there was:
options: Sennacherib's palace, with long series of carved wall reliefs
the tomb of Ashurbanipal, with his body and his golden crown
the city's water clock and a library of papyrus scrolls
a temple of Zeus built by Alexander the Great
questions.explanation: Layard uncovered dozens of rooms of Sennacherib's Southwest Palace and many reliefs, including the Lachish series, which went to the British Museum. No Assyrian royal tomb has been found at Nineveh.

questions.stem: Layard often dug tunnels along the walls of palace rooms, following the carved slabs rather than clearing whole areas. What was the main result for later historians?
options: Reliefs were recovered, but much of their context was lost
Every object was recorded in place, so the palace could be fully rebuilt on paper
The tunnels caused the whole mound to collapse and bury the reliefs again
Nothing at all was recovered from the palace rooms until the twentieth century
questions.explanation: Tunnelling was fast and cheap and produced spectacular sculptures for museums, but it missed floor deposits, stratigraphy and the setting of finds. Modern excavation clears and records whole areas layer by layer.

questions.stem: Hormuzd Rassam, born in Mosul and once Layard's assistant, found the North Palace of Ashurbanipal in 1853. Among his best-known finds were:
options: the gold treasures from the royal tombs at Ur
the reliefs of Ashurbanipal's lion hunts
the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
the Code of Hammurabi on its basalt stele
questions.explanation: Rassam's discoveries in the North Palace included the lion hunt reliefs now in the British Museum. The Black Obelisk came from Nimrud, the Hammurabi stele from Susa, and the Ur treasures from Woolley's later work.

questions.stem: Rassam dug in part of Kuyunjik that had been assigned to the French, working at night. This episode shows that nineteenth-century excavation in Assyria was:
options: focused on recording the daily life of ordinary Assyrian people
driven partly by rivalry between European powers to fill their museums
carefully controlled by international heritage law and charters
led mainly by Iraqi archaeologists working for the Ottoman local government
questions.explanation: British and French teams competed to send sculptures to the British Museum and the Louvre. Heritage charters and Iraqi-led archaeology came much later.

questions.stem: In 1872 George Smith of the British Museum caused a sensation when he identified a tablet from Nineveh that contained:
options: the earliest recorded game of chess
a flood story very like the account of Noah in the Bible
a letter from Sennacherib to the king of Egypt
a map of the known world showing Assyria at its centre
questions.explanation: Smith recognised part of the flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh among the library tablets, and a newspaper then paid for him to go to Nineveh, where he found more fragments. The find fed public interest in Assyria and the Bible.

questions.stem: Early excavators packed thousands of library tablets into crates without recording exactly where each one was found. What problem does this create for historians today?
options: It is impossible to read the tablets, since the cuneiform was damaged in transit
It means the tablets cannot be shown to come from Nineveh at all
It proves the library was a modern forgery made by the excavators
It is hard to reconstruct how the library was organised and where it was kept
questions.explanation: Tablets from the palaces of Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal and other buildings were mixed together, so scholars cannot be sure how the collection was arranged. The texts can still be read, and many carry colophons naming Ashurbanipal.

questions.stem: In 1855 many Assyrian sculptures being shipped to Paris were lost when rafts sank in the Tigris near Qurnah. This shows that early excavation:
options: removed finds quickly, with little thought for their safety
kept every sculpture in place at the site for later study
was carried out only by trained conservators using modern methods
deliberately destroyed sculptures that museums did not want
questions.explanation: The Qurnah disaster sank a large shipment of antiquities bound for the Louvre, a loss made worse because many pieces were poorly recorded. Careful in-situ conservation is a much later approach.

questions.stem: Excavations at the Halzi Gate about 1990, by a team led by David Stronach, found skeletons of people killed in the gateway. Why is this evidence important?
options: It proves that Nineveh was abandoned peacefully before 612 BCE
It shows that the gates were used only as tombs for kings
It confirms that the Greeks besieged Nineveh soon after Alexander's death
It gives physical evidence of fighting at the walls as the city fell
questions.explanation: Bodies left unburied in a gate passage, among weapons, point to a violent assault, which matches the Babylonian account of the fall. The Greeks had no part in the destruction of Nineveh.

questions.stem: Between 2014 and 2016 the group calling itself Islamic State damaged parts of Nineveh. Which statement is correct?
options: It rebuilt Sennacherib's palace as a museum for visitors
It blew up the Nebi Yunus shrine and bulldozed reconstructed gates
It removed the lion hunt reliefs from the British Museum
It drained the Tigris to expose the remains of the ancient harbour
questions.explanation: The shrine on Nebi Yunus was destroyed in 2014 and gates such as the Mashki and Adad gates were bulldozed. Tunnels dug by looters beneath Nebi Yunus later revealed parts of an Assyrian palace that archaeologists have since recorded.

questions.stem: Under Sennacherib, Nineveh was enclosed by a wall about 12 kilometres long. The wall was pierced by:
options: about fifteen named gates
a single gate facing the river
two gates, one for each mound
more than a hundred small gates
questions.explanation: Sennacherib's inscriptions name some fifteen gates, such as the Nergal, Shamash and Adad gates, many named after gods. Several were excavated and partly reconstructed in the twentieth century.

questions.stem: The walls of Neo-Assyrian palace rooms at Nineveh were lined with:
options: carved stone slabs showing the king's deeds
painted wooden panels showing scenes from Greek myths
mosaics of coloured glass showing gods
bronze plates engraved with law codes
questions.explanation: Rooms were lined with large carved slabs, usually of local gypsum, often called orthostats. Traces of paint show that many reliefs were originally coloured.

questions.stem: Sennacherib's reliefs often show a single scene spread across a whole wall, with soldiers, rivers, hills and trees. Compared with earlier palace reliefs at Kalhu, this style:
options: set events in detailed landscapes, telling stories more continuously
showed only gods and never living kings or soldiers
abandoned carving in favour of painted plaster with no carved relief at all
used only abstract patterns without any human figures
questions.explanation: Earlier Kalhu reliefs were often arranged in registers with a band of text between them, while many of Sennacherib's reliefs fill the slab with a landscape and crowds of figures. Kings, soldiers and captives are central to both.

questions.stem: The lion hunt reliefs from Ashurbanipal's North Palace show lions released from cages and killed by the king. Historians usually interpret them as:
options: a joke made by the sculptors at the expense of the king
royal display of the king's duty to protect his land from chaos
a record of how Assyrians farmed lions for their meat and skins
proof that lions had wiped out the farms around the city
questions.explanation: Lion hunting was a royal duty in Assyrian ideology, showing the king defending order against chaos, and the staged hunt in an arena made it a public spectacle. The dying lions are carved with striking realism.

questions.stem: Sennacherib's face on the Lachish relief appears to have been deliberately hacked away. Which interpretation is most widely given?
options: Layard removed the face to sell it to a private collector
Enemies probably defaced his image when Nineveh was sacked
Sennacherib ordered his own face removed after losing the war
The sculptors left it unfinished because the king died
questions.explanation: Damage aimed at the faces of Assyrian kings is widely thought to be the work of attackers in 612 BCE, destroying the power of the royal image. The exact culprits are not known, so this remains an interpretation.

questions.stem: On the mound of Nebi Yunus, Sennacherib and Esarhaddon built an arsenal, or 'review palace'. Its main purpose was to:
options: hold the temple of Ishtar and its festivals
store weapons, chariots and horses and muster the army
house the royal library and train new scribes
serve as the tomb of the prophet Jonah in Assyrian times
questions.explanation: The arsenal was where equipment was kept and troops and horses were inspected before campaigns, showing Nineveh's role as a military centre. The Jonah shrine was built on the mound much later.

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows Nineveh's role as the political centre of the Assyrian Empire in the seventh century BCE?
options: Letters and reports from across the empire found in its palaces
Coins minted at Nineveh and used in every province of the empire
A senate house where elected provincial delegates met each year
Greek inscriptions describing Nineveh as the capital of Persia
questions.explanation: Thousands of letters and administrative texts from officials, governors and spies were sent to the king at Nineveh. Assyria did not use coinage, and it had no elected senate.

questions.stem: Ashurbanipal's colophons and letters show that he had tablets copied and collected from Babylonian temples for his library. This tells us that he:
options: wanted to destroy all Babylonian writing and replace it
could not read, so he relied on Babylonian kings to rule for him
used the tablets only as building material for his palace
valued learning and omen texts as tools of wise kingship
questions.explanation: Ashurbanipal claimed to have learned the scribal art, and his library gathered omens, rituals, literature and scholarly lists, many from Babylonia. Knowledge of omens helped the king make decisions that pleased the gods.

questions.stem: In 689 BCE, after years of revolts, Sennacherib:
options: moved his capital to Babylon
destroyed the city of Babylon
made peace with Egypt
founded the city of Persepolis
questions.explanation: Sennacherib sacked and flooded Babylon after his son, whom he had made its ruler, was handed over to the Elamites by Babylonian rebels. His successor Esarhaddon later began to rebuild it.

questions.stem: Under Ashurbanipal, Assyrian armies sacked Thebes in Egypt in the 660s BCE. Assyrian relations with Egypt at this time are best described as:
options: a struggle for control, with Assyrian-imposed rulers breaking away
a lasting alliance of equals in which Egypt paid no tribute to Assyria
peaceful trade, as Assyria never sent armies into Africa
Egyptian rule over Assyria after the sack of Nineveh
questions.explanation: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt, sacked Thebes and installed local rulers, but Egypt soon regained independence under Psamtik I. Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes, not to Egypt.

questions.stem: Reliefs from Nineveh show the Battle of Til-Tuba, in which Ashurbanipal's army defeated the Elamite king Teumman, whose head was taken to Nineveh. What were these reliefs mainly meant to do?
options: Warn visitors and subjects of the fate of the king's enemies
Record the losses of the Assyrian army for the soldiers' widows
Show that Elam had become an equal ally of Assyria
Honour Teumman as a brave enemy who deserved respect
questions.explanation: Displayed in the palace, scenes of defeated enemies were propaganda aimed at foreign envoys and the court. The same campaign appears in the garden relief, where Teumman's head hangs in a tree.

questions.stem: The Babylonian Chronicle records the fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE. Which detail does it give?
options: The city surrendered at once without any fighting at all
Nineveh was destroyed by an earthquake before the siege began
The Greeks led the siege and carried off the royal library
The city was besieged for about three months before it fell
questions.explanation: The chronicle says the Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes under Cyaxares besieged Nineveh for about three months and plundered it. An Assyrian remnant fled to Harran and fought on for a few more years.

questions.stem: Later Greek writers, following Ctesias, said a flood of the river breached Nineveh's walls and the last king burned himself in his palace. How should historians treat this account?
options: As an eyewitness report written by a Greek soldier inside the city
As the official Assyrian record of the city's last days
As fully confirmed by the excavations at the Halzi Gate
As a late, partly legendary tradition to test against archaeology
questions.explanation: Ctesias wrote centuries later at the Persian court and his work survives through later writers such as Diodorus. Some scholars think water played a role in the attack, but the story of the burning king is legendary.

questions.stem: The Hebrew Bible represents Nineveh in two main ways. Which pairing is correct?
options: Jonah: the capital of the Persians; Nahum: the city where Abraham was born
Jonah: a city destroyed by fire from heaven; Nahum: a city of peace
Jonah: a Greek colony; Nahum: an Egyptian fortress on the Nile
Jonah: a great city that repents; Nahum: a cruel city whose fall is hailed
questions.explanation: In the Book of Jonah the people of Nineveh repent and are spared, while the Book of Nahum rejoices at its coming fall. Biblical images of Assyria strongly shaped how Europeans saw Nineveh before excavation.

questions.stem: The scholar Stephanie Dalley has argued that the famous Hanging Gardens were not in Babylon. What is her claim?
options: They were built by the Romans in Egypt and never existed anywhere in Asia
They were a Greek myth with no basis in any real garden
They were at Persepolis and were built by Darius I
They were Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh, later confused with Babylon's
questions.explanation: Dalley points to Sennacherib's descriptions of his gardens and water-raising works, the garden reliefs and the absence of evidence at Babylon. Many scholars remain unconvinced, so the question is still debated.

questions.stem: When Xenophon's Greek army passed the ruins of Nineveh about 401 BCE, he described an abandoned city without naming it Nineveh. This suggests that:
options: Xenophon had been ordered by the Persian king to keep its name a secret
the city had not yet been built when Xenophon passed by
about two centuries later the city lay in ruin and obscurity
Nineveh was still the busy capital of Assyria at that time
questions.explanation: Xenophon called the ruins Mespila and gave a local story about them, showing how far Nineveh's memory had faded locally after 612 BCE. Assyria as a state had ended two centuries earlier.

questions.stem: Delacroix's painting The Death of Sardanapalus (1827) shows a legendary Assyrian king amid luxury and destruction. Such works mainly reflect:
options: accurate knowledge of Nineveh gained from Layard's excavations of its palaces
Assyrian palace reliefs copied directly by the artist in Iraq
the official history of Assyria written by its own scribes
European Romantic ideas of a decadent East, drawn from Greek legend
questions.explanation: The painting was based on Greek legend and Byron's play, and it came before the excavations of the 1840s. It tells us more about European views of the East than about Assyria.
